title: Asia-Pacific Cybercrime Losses Hit $88 Billion as Scam Gangs Outpace Law Enforcement
excerpt: A new UNODC report finds scam losses across Asia-Pacific at least tripled from 2023 levels, with syndicates using AI and expanding operations to Africa and the Pacific Islands.
body:
• Scam gangs defrauded Asia-Pacific residents of between $88.3 billion and $114.1 billion in 2025, at least tripling losses estimated for 2023.
  • Transnational crime syndicates are adopting agentic AI, relocating to weak-governance territories, and operating like corporate franchises, according to UNODC.
  • People from at least 80 countries have been identified in Southeast Asian scam compounds, many of them trafficked workers held in oppressive conditions.
  • China, South Korea, and Taiwan reported the largest individual country losses, each running into billions of dollars.

Transnational crime syndicates defrauded residents across Asia-Pacific of at least $88 billion in 2025, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime said on Tuesday, warning that organized criminal networks are evolving faster than law enforcement can respond.

The UNODC's latest report estimated combined scam losses across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia, and New Zealand at between $88.3 billion and $114.1 billion for the year — a figure that exceeds the GDP of several nations in the region and represents at least a threefold increase from the $18 billion to $37 billion estimated for 2023.

A Criminal Economy Operating Like a Franchise

Southeast Asia remains the epicentre of the global cyberfraud industry, with mostly Chinese-origin syndicates running operations from fortified compounds in Cambodia, Myanmar, the Philippines, and Laos. But the UNODC report documents a fundamental shift in how these networks operate.

"Their operating model looks like corporate franchising: imagine specialized departments for laundering money, trafficking people, smuggling migrants, and harvesting data, all plugged into the same, service-based interconnected network."

— Delphine Schantz, UNODC Regional Representative for Southeast Asia and the Pacific

Rather than trafficking physical goods, criminal organizations have shifted toward providing reusable criminal services — fraud platforms, payment mechanisms, harvested personal data, and money-laundering infrastructure that can support multiple illegal operations simultaneously. This makes the ecosystem far more resilient. Shutting down one compound or arresting one group disrupts a single operation without dismantling the service layer that enabled it.

Displacement, Not Dismantlement

Law enforcement pressure in traditional hotspots like Myanmar and Laos has pushed operations outward, but has not broken them. Gangs are engaging in what the report calls "jurisdiction shopping," relocating to East Timor, Pacific Island states, and parts of Africa where governance is weak and regulation thin.

Recruitment networks have expanded well beyond Asia. UNODC identified advertisements targeting people with German, Polish, Dutch, Spanish, Italian, French, Swedish, Norwegian, and English language skills. People from at least 80 countries and territories have been found in scam compounds across the region, many of them trafficked workers confined in oppressive environments.

The scale of human trafficking powering these operations remains staggering. Many scam centres are staffed by foreign nationals lured with promises of legitimate jobs, then held against their will and forced to defraud victims worldwide. In October 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice unsealed an indictment against a Cambodian national accused of leading an organization that ran forced-labour scam compounds, and filed a civil forfeiture complaint seeking seizure of approximately $15 billion in bitcoin linked to the fraud.

AI Is Making Scams Harder to Detect

Criminal groups are already using generative AI to create convincing content for fraud schemes. The UNODC report warns the next phase will be worse: syndicates are expected to adopt agentic AI systems capable of autonomously identifying victims, conducting social-engineering campaigns, and facilitating cryptocurrency theft and laundering.

"The scale and complexity of this expanding organised crime economy are outpacing existing responses, which were not structured to address such sophisticated criminal activity."

— Inshik Sim, Lead Analyst, UNODC

The scam sector's rapid growth has fuelled an ecosystem of ancillary criminal services including underground banking and data trading. Investment fraud, particularly so-called "pig butchering" schemes — where victims are groomed over weeks or months before being convinced to invest in fraudulent cryptocurrency platforms — accounts for the bulk of losses. China, South Korea, and Taiwan reported the largest country-level losses in the region, each amounting to billions of dollars, according to the report.

Indians Among Those Trapped

The crisis has direct implications for the Indian diaspora. Indian nationals have been among those trafficked to scam compounds in Myanmar, with India's embassy issuing repeated warnings about fraudulent job offers in Southeast Asia. In one case documented earlier this year, four Indians trapped in Myanmar's Myawaddy scam hub were repatriated after embassy intervention. The UNODC report notes that recruitment networks now operate through transit hubs in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa — corridors commonly used by Indian migrant workers.

India's cybercrime reporting portal, I4C, has flagged a surge in complaints from citizens targeted by online investment and romance scams originating from Southeast Asian operations. For Indians abroad, particularly those in the Gulf states and Southeast Asia, awareness of these recruitment traps is critical.

What's Next

The UNODC has called on governments to coordinate cross-border responses, strengthen financial regulation, and invest in dismantling the service infrastructure that enables these operations rather than targeting individual compounds. The report identified corruption as the "primary enabler" of tech-driven organized crime in the region.

Whether governments can mount a response that matches the speed and sophistication of these criminal networks remains an open question. The syndicates have shown they can move faster than regulators, relocate faster than law enforcement, and adapt faster than the technology platforms trying to shut them down.
